cards.headline: US annual inflation rate rose to 3.7% in September

pages.text: According to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics released on Wednesday, US price increases reached an annual rate of 3.7% in September, up from 3.4% in August. This represents the highest inflation rate since the annual rate reached a three-year peak of 4.2% in May. The report comes ahead of the midterm elections and amid polls showing widespread dissatisfaction with the Trump administration regarding the cost of living. The Guardian World reports that price increases this year have been largely driven by the US-Israel war with Iran, which has caused energy prices to rise. Gasoline accounted for over half of overall price increases, rising 34% from last year, while fuel oil increased by 74% from last year. Additionally, air travel increased by 22.4%.

Overall consumer prices rose 0.6% from August. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, increased by 0.3% in September to an annual rate of 2.6%. Data from AAA indicates that average gas prices remain more than a dollar per gallon higher than last year, while diesel reached a record high last month.

cards.headline: Dalit women in Bangladesh seek security to contest elections

pages.text: At a roundtable discussion in Dhaka, Bangladesh, on October 11, 2026, Dalit women identified several obstacles preventing them from becoming election candidates. Participants, including Sonamoni Modak from Keraniganj and Sathi Sarkar, stated that insecurity and a lack of support are primary concerns. Modak expressed interest in contesting a reserved seat for women in future local government elections but noted that influential local candidates often use intimidation to discourage such attempts. Sarkar added that Dalit women cannot contest elections without assurances of security and support. Other women, Lipi Sarkar, Tithi Mondol, and Shampa Rani Das, cited insecurity, lack of political party support, family opposition, and derogatory societal remarks as barriers to candidacy. The event, titled “Dalit women’s rights in local government elections: Challenges and the way forward,” was organized by the non-governmental organization Avijan and Prothom Alo, with support from the Government of Sweden and technical assistance from the International Foundation for Electoral Systems (IFES). A keynote paper presented at the discussion estimated the Dalit population in Bangladesh to be between 5.5 million and 6.5 million people across more than 50 communities, noting that these groups face discrimination based on ancestry and occupation.

During the discussion, Prime Minister’s Political Adviser Zahir Uddin Swapon stated the government is working toward an inclusive political system and urged Dalit communities to present their needs as demands within government initiatives. Prime Minister’s Special Assistant Bijon Kanti Sarkar noted that while past local government elections were influenced by a particular political party, the government has decided future local elections will not be held on a party basis. Sarkar stated there is no legal barrier to participation and that Dalit women should be able to participate without fear. Three women MPs from the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) also spoke at the event. Newaz Halima Arly cautioned against using disadvantaged Dalit women merely as a vote bank, while Madhabi Marma suggested that opportunities to contest local elections should be provided based on the population of Dalit women in respective areas and emphasized the need to change patriarchal attitudes.

cards.headline: Scientists propose regulatory solutions to mitigate risks of the global pet trade

pages.text: Scientists argue that the global pet trade, specifically involving exotic reptiles and amphibians, poses significant risks to biodiversity and potential human health. In a commentary published in the journal Nature, Susan Lieberman, vice president for international policy at the U.S.-based Wildlife Conservation Society, and Sandra Altherr, co-founder and head of science at Pro Wildlife in Germany, suggest that these risks could be reduced quickly if governments implement specific regulatory changes. Lieberman described the international wildlife trade for species such as reptiles and amphibians as a massive experiment regarding the movement of diseases between different parts of the world. Altherr stated that the exotic pet trade could be regulated very quickly to reduce these risks. The experts identified several legal gaps that governments could address, including the lack of legal recourse for countries of origin when species are sold outside their borders. They also argued that the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) often fails to take proactive approaches to protect species before they become threatened, noting that species nearing extinction may not have sufficient time to undergo the CITES listing process. Additionally, the experts noted that international enforcement and penalties for wildlife trafficking remain weak, with Altherr stating that serious offenses often result in little more than fines and that smugglers face high profits with almost zero risk of jail sentences.

cards.headline: MI5 chief says Russia attempted to interfere in Brexit referendum with little impact

pages.text: Ken McCallum, the head of Britain’s domestic intelligence agency MI5, stated on Tuesday that Moscow attempted to interfere in the 2016 Brexit referendum through social media and television reports, but noted a significant difference between what was attempted and what actually resulted. During an annual threat update, the spy chief reported that Russian-owned English-language broadcasters RT and Sputnik provided biased anti-migration and anti-EU coverage around the time of the referendum. He also identified a second line of attempted interference involving an unspecified number of internet trolls using fake social media accounts, operating largely on X, to influence the result.

Previous studies have cited these interference attempts. The digital campaign group 89up reported that RT and Sputnik published 261 mostly misleading articles regarding immigration and anti-EU issues, which achieved 134 million potential page impressions. Other studies have reported on a state-linked Russian ``troll army'' tweeting about the referendum, though estimates of the number of active accounts have varied between 54 and 150,000. McCallum endorsed comments made by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who raised the issue of Russian interference over the past two days, though McCallum cautioned that continuing the debate risked providing the Kremlin with a needless propaganda victory.

pages.text: Ghanaian Minister of Finance, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, is leading a delegation to the 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group in Bangkok, Thailand. Scheduled for October 12–18, 2026, the meetings involve finance ministers, central bank governors—including the Governor of the Bank of Ghana, Dr Johnson Pandit Asiama—and other senior global officials to address pressing global economic challenges. According to Graphic Online, this gathering is the first held outside Washington, D.C., since Dr Forson assumed office in 2025. The meetings occur as Ghana prepares to transition from economic stabilisation toward sustained transformation following the conclusion of its $3 billion bailout programme. Dr Forson is expected to engage in bilateral and multilateral discussions with IMF leadership, senior World Bank officials, and other international financial institutions and development partners to reassure investors regarding Ghana's economic outlook and commitment to reforms.

cards.headline: Annual job creation in Bangladesh lags behind labor market entry, World Bank report finds

cards.headline: Study finds scientists with high faith in technology less likely to take climate action

pages.text: A study from the London School of Economics, published in Environmental Research Letters, found that scientists who believe technology will largely solve the problems caused by the climate crisis are less likely to engage in civic action or lifestyle changes. The research surveyed more than 9,000 scientists across 115 countries regarding their views on “techno-optimism.” Of those surveyed, 27% agreed that technology will largely solve climate change problems, while 44% disagreed and 29% neither agreed nor disagreed. The report found that techno-optimism was most prevalent among scientists working in applied and natural sciences and those with right-leaning political views. Lead author Fabian Dablander stated that the belief in technological solutions can lead to an over-reliance on unproven solutions at the expense of necessary socioeconomic transformations, noting that technological solutions are often politically attractive because they do not require changes to how people live and consume.

According to the London School of Economics report, “techno-optimist” scientists are 23% less likely to sign petitions or participate in protests than peers who doubt technology is the answer. These scientists also reported engaging in less advocacy and fewer civic actions. Additionally, the study found that techno-optimists are 18% less likely to make high-impact lifestyle changes, such as reducing flights, cutting car usage, or adopting a mostly vegan or vegetarian diet. Dablander noted that while technology cannot substitute for broader societal changes and large-scale shifts in consumption, there is a tendency at the individual level for greater faith in technological solutions to go hand in hand with less engagement in climate action.

cards.headline: Study finds land use changes after colonisation created a wildfire loop in south-east Australia

pages.text: Researchers have identified a “catastrophic wildfire loop” in south-east Australia, where land use changes following colonisation have increased susceptibility to climate-fuelled bushfires. According to a study published in Nature, the shift from open woodland to dense forest after 1788 led to more intense fires, a change consistent with the removal of the Gunaikurnai people from the land and the subsequent loss of cultural burning practices. Michael-Shawn Fletcher, a professor at the University of Melbourne and the study’s lead author, stated that land use changes occurred more than a century before climate changes, allowing shrubs to increase and fires to become hotter. These intense fires then trigger eucalypt recruitment, which in turn drives further fire. The research was conducted by a team working with the Gunaikurnai Land and Waters Aboriginal Corporation, an organisation representing traditional owners. The team reconstructed 1,000 years of vegetation and fire history at Purghagoolah, a lake in Croajingolong National Park in Gippsland, Victoria, by analysing pollen and charcoal particles in a metre-long sediment core. Fletcher noted that prior to colonisation, the area was a “cared for and managed landscape.” Cultural burning involves First Nations people using low-temperature fire to maintain landscapes through a “right time, right place” approach, which differs from government hazard reduction practices. While these practices are still used in parts of Australia as of October 7, 2026, Fletcher suggested the research provides scientific evidence for integrating Indigenous knowledge into modern fire management. Adam Morton, a fire scientist at the University of Tasmania who was not an author of the paper, described the research as significant to the understanding of landscape change resulting from the loss of Indigenous fire management.

cards.headline: Two scientists awarded 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discoveries regarding mirror-image molecules

pages.text: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced in Stockholm, Sweden, on Wednesday that the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry has been awarded to Henri B Kagan of Paris-Sud University in France and Kensō Soai of Tokyo University of Science in Japan. The scientists received the prize for the discovery of nonlinear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis, which demonstrated how chemical reactions can produce an overwhelming excess of one of two mirror-image forms of a molecule. The two recipients will each receive an equal share of a 12 million Swedish kronor prize, valued at approximately £900,000. This property, known as chirality, allows molecules to exist in two forms that contain the same atoms but act as mirror images of one another. While laboratory reactions typically produce equal quantities of both forms, the chemistry underpinning life is homochiral, meaning it is same-handed; for example, proteins are built almost exclusively from L-amino acids. Prof Andre Cobb, an organic chemist at King’s College London, noted that because many molecules in the body are chiral, the different versions of a drug can interact with the body in different ways, potentially leading to weakened or different drug effects. The drug thalidomide was cited as a potent example of these differing interactions.

Rahman also addressed the media environment under previous leaderships. He recalled the Awami League era, during which journalists were jailed and Prothom Alo faced sustained pressure. He noted that deposed prime minister Sheikh Hasina had labeled Prothom Alo an “enemy” of the party and the country in parliament. Rahman stated that before the 2024 uprising, military intelligence placed “tremendous pressure” on Prothom Alo to oust him and relinquish ownership. He remarked that if that government had lasted longer, the company's management could have been taken away. Rahman further observed that the media industry became increasingly unstable, with pressure from various groups forcing management changes and leaving journalists jobless, leading to an atmosphere of uncertainty and self-censorship. He also noted that on December 18, 2025, protests by extremists and what he termed “hateful propaganda” culminated in the vandalism and arson attacks on the offices of both Prothom Alo and The Daily Star.

cards.headline: UAE prosecutor says Flydubai co-pilot used crash axe in attempted terrorist attack

pages.text: United Arab Emirates prosecutor general Hamad Saif al-Shamsi stated that the co-pilot of Flydubai flight FZ1073 attempted to carry out a “terrorist attack” using a crash axe. The incident occurred on September 30, 2026, during an Israel-bound flight carrying 182 people. According to Al-Shamsi, the axe is an implement typically kept inside the cockpit for emergencies, such as fires or crashes, and would not have required covert smuggling. The aircraft plunged 16,625ft in just over 30 seconds during the event, a descent so extreme that part of the rudder was ripped off. A disaster was narrowly averted when passengers and crew intervened to stop the co-pilot's attempt to take control of the plane. The Flydubai captain, identified as Indian national Smit Machchhar, reported that he used his remaining energy to unlock the cockpit door, allowing others to enter, subdue the co-pilot, and stabilize the aircraft. Machchhar sustained wounds to his head, hands, and neck. Both the captain and co-pilot were taken to the UAE for medical treatment following immediate care in Saudi Arabia.

Media outlets have identified the co-pilot as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national. Reports from the Wall Street Journal and the Associated Press indicate that al-Hammami had previously been barred from flying by Oman due to concerns regarding extremist views, after which he was moved to an administrative role at Oman Air before being hired by Flydubai. It remains unclear to what extent he was vetted during the hiring process. Investigations are ongoing to determine if al-Hammami acted as a “lone wolf” or had connections to extremist groups. On October 2, 2026, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stated that the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radicalization,” though he provided no evidence. Security agencies from four regional countries, including Israel, are working to establish motives with assistance from the United States and other Western governments. A Flydubai spokesperson confirmed on Saturday that the incident remains under investigation.

cards.headline: US Air Force redeploys bombers from RAF Fairford in England following suspected terror attack investigation

pages.text: The US Air Force has redeployed all bombers stationed at RAF Fairford, a US-run military air base in England, back to their home stations in the United States. According to a Pentagon official speaking on condition of anonymity on October 4, 2026, the movement follows an investigation into a planned terror attack at the base. A Pentagon spokesperson acknowledged the redeployment, noting that operational security precluded real-time confirmation of asset movements. Aviation observers, including the Military Air Tracking Alliance, had previously noted dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of the Gloucestershire base since the start of the Iran war. On October 4, 2026, observers noted at least 10 of 12 B-1 bombers flying out of the base, including some that had arrived on rotation less than a week prior. This rapid departure follows a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September and the subsequent arrest of a dual British-Iranian national in central London on suspicion of plotting a terror attack. In total, six people have been taken into custody and released on bail during the investigation. British authorities have linked the incident to Tehran, though Iran has denied involvement.

The withdrawal occurs as President Donald Trump weighs options regarding the war in Iran. On October 3, 2026, while leaving the White House for a rally in Ohio, Trump told reporters, “We have decisions that I’ll make about Iran. Iran’s been decimated. So the only question is — it’ll either be the easy way, or the hard way.” RAF Fairford, located 100 miles west of London, has been used by American bombers for decades during Middle East conflicts. While the UK Ministry of Defence provided no immediate comment, reporting suggests the withdrawal appears to be a response to security concerns regarding the safety of the base.

cards.headline: US Vice-President JD Vance aligns with Make America Healthy Again movement

pages.text: US Vice-President JD Vance, a widely considered Republican frontrunner for the 2028 presidential election, is aligning himself with the Make America Healthy Again (Maha) movement, according to reporting by The Guardian World. At a Maha summit in Washington, DC, on September 29, 2026, Vance engaged with Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and leader of Maha, discussing topics such as memes and the “carnivore” diet. Vance has positioned himself as the inheritor of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, and his attachment to Maha signals an overlap between the two movements as the administration's popularity declines amid rising prices and the war in Iran. Art Caplan, professor emeritus at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, noted that Vance underlined the politics being stirred up by Maha during the event. While Kennedy spoke regarding the inefficiencies of the US health system compared to European universal healthcare, Vance highlighted his role leading an anti-fraud task force. Vance claimed the task force has identified close to $250bn in fraud within Medicaid, Medicare, and the Affordable Care Act marketplace, alleging that undocumented immigrants are receiving benefits. The administration has released few details regarding why specific individuals were unenrolled from these programs or the nature of the alleged fraud, and there is no documentation currently available to support the claim that undocumented people are receiving Medicare benefits.

cards.headline: Iran says Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until seven conditions are met

pages.text: Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf stated on Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until seven conditions, outlined in an interim understanding reached with the United States last June, are fulfilled. Ghalibaf, speaking via the state-linked news agency Nournews, said the decision follows Tehran receiving a U.S. response to its diplomatic proposal. He noted that Washington recently submitted new proposals through a mediator, despite what he described as differences between those proposals and public statements. Ghalibaf stated that Tehran would no longer accept stalling or the imposition of unilateral demands, asserting that the resumption of navigation through the strait is tied to the fulfillment of conditions based on the Islamabad memorandum of understanding. He added that Iran would both fight and negotiate and is prepared to confront the U.S. with new surprises on the military battlefield. Last week, U.S. President Donald Trump ruled out an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait, which is used to ship one-fifth of global oil and natural gas during peacetime.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told foreign ambassadors and diplomats in Tehran that Iran has clearly explained its conditions for reopening the waterway and hopes Washington will choose diplomacy. Araghchi stated that Iran is serious about finding diplomatic solutions but warned that if the U.S. takes military action again, Iran is more prepared than before and will take necessary action to defend itself. Additionally, Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei noted that Tehran used the United Nations General Assembly platform last month to present its position regarding the end of the U.S.-Israel war on Iran.

cards.headline: BGMEA president urges Pakistan to increase imports from Bangladesh to address trade imbalance

pages.text: Mahmud Hasan Khan, President of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), has urged Pakistan to increase its imports of Bangladeshi products to address an existing trade imbalance. During a bilateral meeting in Uttara, Dhaka, Khan specifically identified high-quality jute yarn and life-saving pharmaceuticals as key sectors for increased exports to Pakistan. He noted that while Bangladesh imports significant volumes of essential raw materials, such as chemicals and dyes for the ready-made garment (RMG) sector, from Pakistan, Bangladeshi exports to Pakistan remain disproportionately low. The meeting included Pakistani High Commissioner to Bangladesh Imran Haidar and took place on a Sunday, though the specific calendar date was not established by the report from The Financial Express Bangladesh. To strengthen economic cooperation, Khan also called for the modernization of logistics to address excessive time required for direct maritime transportation.

In response to the proposals, High Commissioner Imran Haidar expressed interest and assured BGMEA leadership that measures would be taken to boost two-way trade. Haidar suggested the exchange of high-level business delegations to explore market opportunities, stating that the High Commission would organize Business-to-Business (B2B) meetings and matchmaking sessions with Pakistani importers, brands, and trade bodies if a Bangladeshi delegation visits. Discussions also included potential market access strategies, such as formulating a bilateral special Free Trade Agreement (FTA) mechanism to sustain trade flows following Bangladesh's graduation from LDC status under SAFTA. Additionally, the parties discussed institutional development, including technology transfer and student exchange programs between the BGMEA University of Fashion & Technology (BUFT) and Pakistani textile institutes.

cards.headline: Latvia's United List party secures largest parliamentary election victory since independence

pages.text: In Latvia's parliamentary election, the centrist United List party led by Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs secured a historic victory, appearing to win the largest share of votes since the country regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991. Preliminary results indicated that with 97% to 99.9% of ballots counted, the United List earned approximately 35.3% to 35.4% of the vote, granting the party 42 of the 100 seats in the Saeima. The result places Kulbergs, a 47-year-old businessman and amateur rally driver, in a position to form a pro-Ukraine coalition. Kulbergs, who assumed office in May after a previous coalition collapsed following incidents involving stray Ukrainian military drones, stated on the night of October 3, 2026, that he would not cooperate with pro-Russian parties and specifically ruled out a coalition with the populist Latvia First party. Political scientist Roberts Kits noted that the United List could potentially secure a parliamentary majority by partnering with either the left-leaning Progressives or the nationalist National Alliance. The election, which involved 14 parties contesting 100 seats via a proportional system, was shaped by concerns regarding national security and rising living costs. While most parties support high military spending and aid to Kyiv, the Sovereign Power party opposed military aid to Ukraine and increased defense spending, appearing set to finish third. An exit poll placed the populist Latvia First party in second place with 11.3%, nearly double its 2022 share. Both populist parties were noted as benefiting from shifts in voting patterns among Latvia's ethnic Russian-speaking minority.

cards.headline: Toronto Fire Services launches Fire Prevention Week 2026 focusing on safe charging

pages.text: Toronto Fire Services is encouraging residents to prioritize fire safety during Fire Prevention Week 2026, which is scheduled to take place from Sunday, October 4 to October 3, 2026. The theme for this year is “Safe Charging Is a Superpower,” a campaign centered on charging habits intended to help prevent lithium-ion battery fires in homes and communities. Lithium-ion batteries are used in various daily devices, including smartphones, tablets, e-bikes, e-scooters, and other portable electronics. While generally safe when used properly, Toronto Fire Services notes that damaged, defective, or improperly charged batteries can pose a serious fire risk. Jim Jessop, Fire Chief of Toronto Fire Services, stated that safe charging involves using approved equipment and following manufacturer instructions, such as using approved chargers, cords, and batteries, avoiding tampering with or modifying devices, and replacing any damaged or defective charging equipment.
